ox: Incorrect. 12.5 is not in the table. The rows next to 250 are 8.2 (at 100) and 18.3 (at 250); 12.5 would be a guess between them.
Correct. Find the 250 µmol photons row in Table 1. Its mean O₂ rate is 18.3 µmol O₂ m⁻² s⁻¹.
Incorrect. 24.7 is not in the table; the 500 µmol row shows 25.4.
Incorrect. 30.1 is higher than every value in the table (the maximum is 26.1 at 750 µmol).

concept.t: Reading a value from a table
p: For a lookup question, find the row that matches the condition (250 µmol photons) and read the right column (Mean_O2). Values that do not appear anywhere in the table are distractors.

bp972_0.trap: Choosing an interpolated or plausible-looking number that is not in the table.
mem: Match the row first, then read the column.
Mean_O2 = average rate; SD = spread.
Photosynthesis rises with light and then plateaus (saturation).
bp972_0.sc: Underline the row label in the table before looking at the choices.
bp972_0.plain: Look up the row, read across, done.

ox: Wrong. Hexokinase is the first step and traps glucose in the cell as G6P, but G6P can still go to glycogen or the pentose phosphate pathway. It is not the committed step.
Correct. PFK-1 turns fructose-6-phosphate into fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. After this step the sugar is committed to glycolysis. It is slowed by ATP and sped up by AMP and F2,6BP.
Wrong. Pyruvate kinase is regulated, but it is the last step, after the commitment has already been made.
Wrong. This enzyme starts the pentose phosphate pathway, a different route. Do not confuse it with glycolysis.

p: Glycolysis breaks glucose into pyruvate. The committed step is the one after which the molecule has no other option but to continue down the pathway. It is usually also the slowest, regulated step.
In glycolysis this is PFK-1. ATP signals the cell has enough energy and turns it down. AMP signals low energy and turns it up.

mem: PFK-1: F6P to F1,6BP is the committed, rate-limiting step.
ATP and citrate inhibit PFK-1; AMP and F2,6BP activate it.
Hexokinase = first step; pyruvate kinase = last step.
q14.trap: Choosing hexokinase because it is first. First is not the same as committed.
q14.plain: Think of a one-way toll gate on a highway. Once your car goes through, you cannot take any exit but the one ahead.

ox: Correct. Glycolysis makes 4 ATP but spends 2 early on, so the net is 2 ATP. It also makes 2 NADH.
Wrong. 4 ATP is the gross yield. You must subtract the 2 ATP invested in the first steps.
Wrong. About 30-32 ATP is the total from complete aerobic breakdown (glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, TCA cycle, electron transport chain).
Wrong. Glycolysis makes NADH. FADH2 is made in the TCA cycle and in fatty acid oxidation.

p: Glycolysis splits one glucose into two pyruvate. Early steps spend 2 ATP to prepare the sugar. Later steps make 4 ATP.
Net means what is left after paying the cost. It also makes 2 NADH, an electron carrier that can later be used to make more ATP.

mem: Glycolysis net: 2 ATP, 2 NADH, 2 pyruvate.
Gross ATP = 4; invested = 2.
Aerobic total is about 30-32 ATP.

fm.f: Net ATP = ATP made - ATP spent
fm.why: Net yield means profit after the investment.
fm.nc: Simple subtraction.

q15.trap: Reporting the gross 4 ATP instead of the net 2 ATP.
q15.plain: You pay 2 dollars to enter a game and win 4 dollars. You walked away with 2 dollars of profit.

ox: Wrong. Complex I is blocked by rotenone, not cyanide.
Correct. Cyanide binds the iron in complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), so electrons cannot pass to O2. The whole chain backs up and O2 use stops.
Wrong. ATP synthase is blocked by oligomycin. That would stop ATP making but the chain problem is different.
Wrong. Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) is inhibited by malonate, not cyanide.

p: The electron transport chain is a line of protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Electrons are passed down the line and finally given to oxygen at complex IV, forming water.
If complex IV is blocked, electrons cannot leave the chain. Everything upstream backs up and oxygen is no longer used.

mem: Cyanide (and CO, azide) block complex IV.
Rotenone blocks complex I; malonate blocks complex II.
Oligomycin blocks ATP synthase.
q16.trap: Mixing up which poison blocks which complex. Oxygen is the final acceptor, so the O2-related poison hits complex IV.
q16.plain: It is like a bucket line passing water to the end person. If the last person is stuck, the whole line stops.

ox: Correct. A proton leak is an uncoupler. The gradient cannot build, so the chain runs faster to try to fix it and uses more O2. ATP synthase has little gradient to use, so ATP falls. The energy is lost as heat.
Wrong. Falling O2 use fits an electron transport chain inhibitor such as cyanide. A leak makes the chain work harder, not slower.
Wrong. ATP synthesis needs the proton gradient. If protons leak back, there is less drive to make ATP.
Wrong. Glycolysis makes only 2 net ATP and cannot make up the loss. Also, the ETC and gradient are directly affected.

p: The electron transport chain pumps protons out of the matrix to build a gradient. Protons flow back through ATP synthase, which makes ATP. This links (couples) O2 use to ATP making.
An uncoupler lets protons leak back in without passing through ATP synthase. The chain speeds up, O2 use rises, ATP falls, and the extra energy becomes heat.

mem: Uncoupler: O2 use up, ATP down, heat up.
Examples: DNP, thermogenin (UCP1) in brown fat.
Inhibitors of the ETC lower O2 use.
q17.trap: Thinking less ATP always means less O2 use. Uncouplers speed up O2 use.
q17.plain: Picture a water wheel with a hole in the pool above. The pump works nonstop to refill the pool, but the wheel barely turns.

ox: Wrong. CoA attaches to the fatty acid in the cytosol but the acyl-CoA cannot cross the inner membrane by itself.
Correct. Carnitine swaps places with CoA, carries the acyl group across, and CoA is reattached in the matrix, where beta-oxidation occurs.
Wrong. Albumin carries free fatty acids through the blood, not across the mitochondrial membrane.
Wrong. Chylomicrons carry dietary fat from the gut through lymph and blood.

p: Beta-oxidation, the breakdown of fatty acids for energy, happens inside the mitochondrial matrix. Long fatty acids must get past the inner mitochondrial membrane, which blocks them.
Carnitine acts as a ferry. It picks up the acyl group, carries it across, and drops it off inside the matrix.

mem: Carnitine carries long-chain acyl groups into the matrix.
CPT-I is the rate-limiting step; malonyl-CoA inhibits it.
Albumin = blood transport; chylomicron = dietary fat transport.
q18.trap: Picking CoA because it is attached to the fatty acid. It activates it but cannot cross.
q18.plain: Carnitine is like a ferry that carries cars across a river where no bridge exists.

ox: Wrong. Liver glycogen runs out within about a day of fasting, so it cannot help by day three.
Correct. Liver turns fatty acids into acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate. These cross the blood-brain barrier, so the brain uses them and needs less glucose.
Wrong. Long-chain fatty acids cannot cross the blood-brain barrier well, so the brain does not use them much.
Wrong. Lactate is recycled to glucose through the Cori cycle, which does not reduce the brain's glucose need.

p: During fasting, the body first uses glycogen, then makes glucose from other sources. Over days, the liver breaks down fat and makes ketone bodies, small molecules that can be burned for energy.
The brain can use ketones, so it needs less glucose. This spares muscle protein from being broken down for glucose.

mem: Ketones: acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate (and acetone).
Made in the liver; used by brain, heart, muscle but not by the liver.
Liver glycogen lasts about 24 hours.
q19.trap: Choosing fatty acids since fat is the source. The brain uses the ketones made from them, not fatty acids directly.
q19.plain: When the gas station is closed, you switch your car to a backup fuel tank.

ox: Wrong. A randomized block design groups subjects by a nuisance trait (a block) and randomizes within each block. The passage describes no blocks, only that discs were assigned to light levels at random.

Correct. The passage says discs were assigned to light levels at random and only one factor was changed (light intensity: 100, 250, 500, 750). Random assignment with one factor and no blocking is a completely randomized design.
Wrong. A factorial design changes two or more factors at once (for example light and temperature). Here only light intensity was varied.
Wrong. Quasi-experimental studies do not randomly assign subjects to groups. The passage states that discs were assigned at random.

p: In a completely randomized design, chance alone decides which group each unit goes into. There are no extra grouping steps.
A block design first sorts units into similar groups, then randomizes inside each group. A factorial design varies more than one factor. A quasi-experiment has no random assignment.

bp972_1.plain: It is like drawing names from a hat to decide who gets which treatment, with no sorting first.
mem: Random assignment plus one factor and no blocks means completely randomized.
Two or more factors varied together means factorial.
No random assignment means quasi-experimental or observational.
Replication (repeating the experiment) is not the same as blocking.
bp972_1.trap: Confusing replication (the experiment was repeated thrice) with a randomized block design.

ox: Wrong. A CV of 5% would need an SD near 1.3 (5% of about 25). The table gives an SD of 1.8, which is larger.
Correct. CV = SD / mean x 100, where SD = 1.8 and mean = 25.4 (the 500 row). 1.8 / 25.4 x 100 is about 7.1%.
Wrong. 15% of 25.4 is about 3.8, which would need an SD more than twice the 1.8 given.
Wrong. 20% of 25.4 is about 5.1, far above 1.8. You would only get near 20% by dividing by a much smaller mean such as 8.2.

p: The coefficient of variation (CV) shows how big the spread is compared with the average. It is the standard deviation (SD) divided by the mean, times 100 to make a percent.
A small CV means the data are tightly clustered around the mean.

bp972_2.plain: A 2 cm wobble matters a lot on a 10 cm pencil but hardly at all on a 2 m pole. CV measures the wobble relative to size.
mem: CV = SD / mean x 100.
Always divide by the mean of the same group.
CV has no units.

fm.f: CV (%) = (SD / mean) x 100, where SD = standard deviation and mean = average of the group
fm.v: SD = 1.8, mean = 25.4 (500 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹)
fm.why: It converts the spread into a percent of the average so groups can be compared.
fm.nc: Round 25.4 to 25. 1.8 / 25 = 0.072, about 7%. Only option B is near that.

bp972_2.sc: Estimate 10% of 25.4 is 2.5. Since 1.8 is a bit smaller than 2.5, the answer is a bit under 10%, which points to 7.1%.
bp972_2.trap: Dividing the SD by the wrong group's mean (1.8/8.2 gives about 22%) or forgetting to divide by the mean.

ox: Correct. This is NOT supported. Table 1 gains are 8.2 to 18.3 (+10.1) over 150 units, 18.3 to 25.4 (+7.1) over 250 units, and 25.4 to 26.1 (+0.7) over 250 units. A linear rise would give equal gain per unit of light, so the trend is saturating, not linear.
Wrong. This IS supported. The rate went from 25.4 at 500 to 26.1 at 750, only +0.7, and the passage says a plateau approaches saturation near 500.
Wrong. This IS supported. 26.1 at 750 is larger than 25.4 at 500 in Table 1, even if only slightly.
Wrong. This IS supported. 8.2 at 100 is the smallest mean in the table.

p: A linear relationship goes up by the same amount for every equal step. A saturating relationship rises fast, then flattens as something else becomes the limit.
In photosynthesis, light drives the process at low levels. At high light, enzymes cannot work faster, so the rate levels off.

bp972_3.plain: Like a checkout line: adding more shoppers speeds things up until the cashier is working as fast as possible.
mem: Shrinking gains per step means curved, not linear.
Saturation: extra light stops helping because another factor limits.
For NOT questions, find the one false statement.
bp972_3.trap: Assuming a steady increase means a linear one, and missing that the gains shrink to +0.7.

ox: Wrong. If light were still limiting, the rate would keep rising with light. From 500 to 750 it rose only 0.7 (25.4 to 26.1), and the passage says the curve plateaus.

Correct. The rate rose from 8.2 to 18.3 early on but only 0.7 from 500 to 750. The passage says beyond a threshold other factors, such as enzyme capacity, become rate-determining, so extra light goes unused.
Wrong. The rate more than doubled from 100 (8.2) to 250 (18.3), so it was not saturated at 100.
Wrong. Photoinhibition would lower the rate at 750. But 26.1 is higher than 25.4, so no fall occurred.

p: A limiting factor is the one thing that caps how fast a process can go. At low light, light is limiting. When light is plentiful, another step, such as the capacity of the enzymes, becomes limiting.
Once that happens, adding more of the first factor changes the rate very little.

bp972_4.plain: A factory with ten helpers cannot make more cars by delivering more parts if the helpers are already as fast as they can go.
mem: Plateau means another factor is now limiting.
Photoinhibition would show a decrease, not a small increase.
Compare the actual numbers before accepting an interpretation.

fm.f: Gain = rate at higher light - rate at lower light
fm.why: A tiny gain shows the rate is near its ceiling.

bp972_4.trap: Assuming more light always means more photosynthesis, so a flat rate must mean damage or error.

ox: Wrong. The passage reports a mean reduction of 4.2 mg/dL, and the table lists -4.2. Glucose went down, not up.
Correct. The supplement group's fasting glucose change was -4.2 mg/dL and placebo was -1.8 mg/dL. The difference is 4.2 - 1.8 = 2.4 mg/dL more reduction, and p < 0.01.
Wrong. The passage reports a statistically significant difference between groups (p < 0.01), so there was an effect.
Wrong. 1.8 mg/dL is the placebo group's own reduction. The supplement's extra effect is 4.2 - 1.8 = 2.4.

p: A placebo is a dummy treatment. Placebo groups often improve a little by themselves. So the real effect of a treatment is the change in the treatment group minus the change in the placebo group.
Here, both groups lowered glucose. The supplement lowered it by more.

bp974_0.plain: If both runners improve their time, you judge the coaching by how much more one improved.
mem: Effect = treatment change - placebo change.
Placebo groups can also change.
p < 0.01 means a statistically significant difference.

fm.f: Net effect = supplement reduction - placebo reduction
fm.why: It removes the improvement that happened without the supplement.

bp974_0.trap: Treating the placebo reduction (1.8) as the treatment effect, or ignoring that placebo also changed.

ox: Wrong. Single-blind means only one side does not know the assignment. It reduces bias but does not balance confounders. The trial was actually double-blind.
Correct. Random assignment to supplement (n = 60) or placebo (n = 60) balances known and unknown confounders between groups, so differences can be attributed to the supplement.
Wrong. The passage describes two parallel groups of 60, not a crossover. A crossover is also not what makes cause clear here.
Wrong. A larger sample (120) improves precision but does not remove bias or confounding by itself.

p: Confounders are other traits (age, diet, weight) that could affect the outcome. Random assignment spreads these about evenly across groups by chance.
Then the main difference between groups is the treatment, so the effect can be linked to it.

bp974_1.plain: Like shuffling a deck before dealing: neither player is favored.
mem: Randomization controls confounders.
Blinding reduces bias in measurement and expectation.
Sample size improves precision, not causation.
bp974_1.trap: Choosing blinding or sample size, which are good features but do not control confounding.

ox: Correct. ARR = rate in treatment group - rate in placebo group = 30% - 15% = 15% = 0.15.
Wrong. 0.30 is just the supplement group's improvement rate. ARR needs the placebo rate subtracted.
Wrong. 0.45 comes from adding 30% and 15%. ARR is a difference, not a sum.
Wrong. 0.60 would be 30% doubled or similar. It has no basis in subtracting 15% from 30%.

p: Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is the difference between the event rate in the control group and in the treatment group. It shows how many more people per 100 benefit.
Here the event is improvement, so the difference is treatment rate minus placebo rate.

bp974_2.plain: If 30 of 100 improve with the pill and 15 of 100 improve with sugar, the pill helped 15 extra people per 100.
mem: ARR = difference between two rates.
Subtract, do not add.
Percent difference of 15 points = 0.15.

fm.f: ARR = rate in supplement group - rate in placebo group
fm.why: It measures the extra improvement caused by the treatment.

bp974_2.trap: Reporting the treatment group's rate alone (0.30) instead of subtracting the placebo rate.

ox: Correct. This is the misinterpretation. The passage reports statistical significance (p < 0.01), but the net reduction is only 4.2 - 1.8 = 2.4 mg/dL, and authors say it may modestly improve control. Statistical significance does not prove clinical significance.
Wrong. This is a correct reading. The passage reports p < 0.01 for the group difference.
Wrong. This is a correct reading. The net difference is 2.4 mg/dL and the authors say further studies are needed for long-term benefit.
Wrong. This is a correct reading. The passage says adverse events were mild and comparable between groups.

p: Statistical significance means a difference is unlikely to be due to chance. Clinical significance means the difference is big enough to matter to a patient's health.
A tiny effect can be statistically significant, especially with many participants.

bp974_3.plain: A scale that detects a 1 gram change is precise, but 1 gram does not change your weight in any way that matters.
mem: p-value tells about chance, not importance.
Effect size judges practical meaning.
Watch for overstatement words like proves or clinically significant.
bp974_3.trap: Treating p < 0.01 as proof that the benefit matters clinically.

ox: Correct. Glucose was measured only at baseline and week 12, and the authors say further studies are needed to confirm long-term benefits and safety. A 12-week trial cannot show lasting effects.
Wrong. Randomization strengthens the causal link and has nothing to do with how long people are followed.
Wrong. A placebo comparator improves the comparison and does not limit follow-up time.
Wrong. Blinding of participants and investigators reduces bias and does not affect duration.

p: Follow-up length decides what you can say about lasting effects and rare or late side effects. A short trial can only describe short-term results.
Features like randomization, blinding and placebo protect against bias but do not extend time.

bp974_4.plain: Judging a car after one week of driving tells you little about how it lasts for ten years.
mem: Short follow-up limits long-term conclusions.
Randomization, blinding, placebo improve internal validity.
The authors' own caveats often hint at the answer.
bp974_4.trap: Picking familiar design terms like randomization or blinding as limitations when they are strengths.

ox: Wrong. 200 gave 12.5 in Table 1, the lowest of the four.
Wrong. 400 gave 18.3, which is below 22.7 and 24.1.
Wrong. 600 gave 22.7. Gains slowed after this point, but 800 is still higher.
Correct. At 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ the mean CO₂ uptake is 24.1, the largest in Table 1. The passage says uptake rose at every intensity.

p: Scan the column of values and pick the biggest. Slowing growth is not the same as decreasing.
The passage says uptake rose at every step, so the last value is the highest.

bp979_0.plain: A runner who gains less speed each lap is still getting faster.
mem: Slower gain still means a gain.
Check the table, not the impression from the text.
bp979_0.trap: Choosing 600 because gains slow at high light, even though 800 still has the highest mean.

ox: Wrong. Leaves from different plants differ in many ways, and uncontrolled light means light cannot be isolated as the cause.
Wrong. In natural sunlight, light changes together with temperature and other factors, so effects are mixed up.
Correct. Varying only light while holding temperature, CO₂ and water constant isolates light as the only difference, so any change in uptake is due to light.
Wrong. A survey gathers opinions, not measurements of photosynthesis.

p: The independent variable is the one you change (light). Controlled variables are kept the same (temperature, CO₂, water). The dependent variable is what you measure (CO₂ uptake).
Controls make sure only the independent variable explains the result.

bp979_1.plain: To test a recipe, change one ingredient at a time and keep the oven the same.
mem: Change one variable, hold the rest constant.
Observational studies cannot isolate cause.
Surveys give opinions, not direct measurements.
bp979_1.trap: Choosing a natural-setting or survey option because it feels realistic, though it leaves other factors uncontrolled.

ox: Wrong. 12.6% does not match the calculation. 4.4 divided by 18.3 is about 24%.
Correct. Percent increase = (new - old) / old x 100 = (22.7 - 18.3) / 18.3 x 100 = 4.4 / 18.3 x 100, about 24.0%.
Wrong. 31.1% does not come from these values. It would need a gain near 5.7 on a base of 18.3.
Wrong. 41.2% is far too large. The gain of 4.4 is less than a quarter of 18.3.

p: Percent increase compares the change to the starting value. Subtract old from new, divide by old, multiply by 100.
The starting value is always the base, here the 400 level.

bp979_2.plain: Going from 10 to 12 is a 20% jump because 2 is one fifth of the starting 10.
mem: Divide by the starting value.
Percent change = change / original x 100.
Check against a quarter: 25% of 18.3 is about 4.6.

fm.f: Percent increase = (new - old) / old x 100, where old = starting value, new = ending value
fm.why: The question asks for relative growth from 400 to 600.
fm.nc: Round 18.3 to 18. A quarter of 18 is 4.5, close to 4.4, so about 24-25%.

bp979_2.sc: A quarter of 18.3 is about 4.6. Our gain of 4.4 is just under that, so just under 25%.
bp979_2.trap: Dividing by the new value (22.7) instead of the starting value (18.3).

ox: Correct. This is NOT supported. Uptake rose from 12.5 at 200 to 18.3 at 400, about 1.46 times, not 2 times. Uptake is not proportional to light.
Wrong. This IS supported. 24.1 at 800 is higher than 12.5 at 200.
Wrong. This IS supported. The gain from 600 to 800 is 1.4, smaller than 5.8 from 200 to 400.
Wrong. This IS supported. 18.3 at 400 is higher than 12.5 at 200.

p: If two things are proportional, doubling one doubles the other. Here light doubled (200 to 400), but uptake only went from 12.5 to 18.3.
Doubling 12.5 would give 25.0, which is higher than 18.3.

bp979_3.plain: Doubling the sugar in tea does not make it twice as sweet once it is already sweet enough.
mem: Doubling input should double output if proportional.
Check by doubling the first value.
Photosynthesis flattens at high light.

fm.f: Expected if proportional = 2 x first value
fm.why: It tests the claim that doubling light doubles uptake.
fm.nc: 12.5 + 12.5 = 25, which is much bigger than 18.3.

bp979_3.trap: Assuming photosynthesis rises in direct proportion to light.

ox: Wrong. The gain from 200 to 400 is 18.3 - 12.5 = 5.8, the largest of the three.
Wrong. The gain from 400 to 600 is 22.7 - 18.3 = 4.4, the middle value.
Correct. The gain from 600 to 800 is 24.1 - 22.7 = 1.4, the smallest of 5.8, 4.4 and 1.4. The passage states the same values.
Wrong. The gains 5.8, 4.4 and 1.4 are all different.

p: To find where growth is smallest, subtract each value from the next one. Then compare the differences.
Shrinking differences show the curve is flattening toward a plateau.

bp979_4.plain: Like checking how many inches a child grew each year, not how tall they are.
mem: Subtract neighbors to get gains.
Equal steps in input do not mean equal steps in output.

fm.f: Gain = uptake at higher light - uptake at lower light
fm.why: The question compares gains between successive light levels.
fm.nc: 24.1 - 22.7 is about 24 - 23 = 1, the clear smallest.

bp979_4.trap: Assuming equal 200-unit light steps give equal uptake steps.

ox: Wrong. At 400 the rate is 12.0 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹, the lowest value in the table, not the highest.
Wrong. At 800 the rate is 22.0, which is less than 31.0 at 1600.
Wrong. At 1200 the rate is 28.0. That is still below 31.0 at 1600, even though the curve is flattening.
Correct. The 1600 row shows a net rate of 31.0 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹, larger than 28.0, 22.0 and 12.0 in the other rows. The passage says the rate keeps rising but more slowly, so there is no drop.

concept.t: Reading the highest value in a table
p: Net photosynthetic rate is how much CO₂ a leaf takes in each second after subtracting what it gives off. A bigger number means the leaf is making more sugar.
To find the highest value, scan the whole column and compare every number. Do not stop at a spot where the curve starts to flatten.

bp987_0.plain: It is like a runner who keeps getting faster, just by smaller amounts each lap. The last lap is still the fastest.
mem: Slowing growth is still growth: values keep rising until they actually fall.
Light saturation means the curve flattens, not that it drops.
Always compare every row before choosing the maximum.
bp987_0.trap: Seeing the gains shrink (10, then 6, then 3) and wrongly thinking the rate peaked earlier.

ox: Wrong. Net photosynthetic rate is measured as a result. It is the outcome, so it is the dependent variable.
Wrong. Stomatal conductance was recorded, not set by the researchers. It is another measured response.
Wrong. Leaf temperature was recorded at each light level. It changed as a result of the light, so it was not manipulated.
Correct. The passage says 'Four light intensities (400, 800, 1200, and 1600...) were applied.' The researchers chose these values, so light intensity is the independent variable.

p: The independent variable is the one the researcher deliberately changes. The dependent variable is the one measured to see the effect.
Ask: what did the experimenter set, and what did they only record? The set one is independent.

bp987_1.plain: If you change the oven temperature and watch how fast cookies bake, temperature is what you control and baking time is what you watch.
mem: Independent = manipulated by the researcher (x-axis).
Dependent = measured outcome (y-axis).
Words like 'were applied' or 'were assigned' point to the independent variable.
bp987_1.mn: DRY MIX: Dependent = Responding variable = Y axis; Manipulated = Independent = X axis.
bp987_1.trap: Picking a variable that changes with light (like temperature) even though it was only recorded, not set.

ox: Correct. Slope = change in rate divided by change in light. Rate goes from 12.0 to 22.0, a rise of 10.0. Light goes from 400 to 800, a rise of 400. So 10.0 / 400 = 0.025.
Wrong. 0.030 does not match 10.0 / 400. It would need a rise of 12 over 400.
Wrong. 0.055 is far too large. It is not 10.0 / 400 and looks like a sum of unrelated numbers.
Wrong. 0.0125 is half the true slope. It comes from dividing 10.0 by 800 instead of by the 400 change in light.

p: Slope tells how much y changes for each 1 unit of x. Here it shows how many µmol of CO₂ the leaf takes up for each extra µmol of photons.
Use the two points given, subtract to get the changes, then divide.

bp987_2.plain: Slope is like miles per hour: how much distance you gain for each hour that passes.
mem: Slope = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1).
Divide by the CHANGE in x (400), not by the endpoint (800).
Units of slope are y-units per x-unit.

fm.f: Slope = (rate at 800 - rate at 400) / (light at 800 - light at 400), where rate is net photosynthetic rate and light is light intensity
fm.v: rate at 400 = 12.0, rate at 800 = 22.0, light at 400 = 400, light at 800 = 800
fm.why: Slope is the change in y over the change in x between the two points.

bp987_2.trap: Dividing by 800 (the second x value) instead of the difference 400, which gives 0.0125.

ox: Correct. Saying the rate rises forever is a misconception. The passage notes that 'the rate of increase diminishes at higher intensities, suggesting a light-saturation point.' The table shows gains of 10.0, 6.0, then 3.0.
Wrong. This is not a misconception. The table shows conductance rising from 0.3 to 0.55 as light rises.
Wrong. This is accurate. Leaf temperature goes from 22.1 to 24.5 °C, a modest rise.
Wrong. This is a true statement, not a misconception. Too much light can damage the photosynthetic machinery, which is called photoinhibition.

p: At low light, more light means more photosynthesis. At higher light, other things such as enzymes and CO₂ supply become the limit, so extra light helps less and less.
This flattening point is called light saturation. Very strong light can even cause damage.

bp987_3.plain: Think of a toll booth: adding more cars per minute helps until the booth can't process any faster.
mem: Light-response curve rises, then plateaus (saturates).
Another factor becomes limiting at saturation.
Excess light can cause photoinhibition.

p: For NOT or EXCEPT questions, check each statement against the table. Three will be true; the false one is the answer.
Different columns can trend differently. Here growth rate peaks and then falls, but yield keeps rising.

bp1008_3.plain: It is like a scoreboard: check each claim against the actual score, one at a time.
mem: Verify each option against the table.
Growth rate peaks at 4,000 lux; yield and height keep rising.
Rate and total are different measures.
bp1008_3.trap: Assuming that because growth rate dropped at 8,000 lux, yield must have dropped too.

ox: Wrong. Photoperiodism is a plant's response to day length (hours of light), but here light intensity was varied, not day length.
Correct. More light gives more energy for photosynthesis, so plants make more sugars, which supports more seed production. Yield rose from 3.1 g to 10.2 g as light rose from 1,000 to 8,000 lux.
Wrong. Photoinhibition is damage from too much light. The passage says it may limit growth rate at 8,000 lux, but yield kept increasing, so it does not explain the rising yield.
Wrong. A circadian rhythm is a roughly 24-hour internal clock. Light was constant in every chamber, so it does not explain differences among them.

p: Photosynthesis is how plants use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugars. More light supplies more energy, up to a limit.
Plants use these sugars to grow and to make seeds. Photoinhibition is damage that can occur at very high light.

bp1008_4.plain: A solar-powered factory makes more products when more sunlight hits its panels, until the panels overheat.
mem: Photosynthesis makes sugars from light, CO2 and water.
Photoperiodism concerns day length, not brightness.
Photoinhibition is damage from excess light.
bp1008_4.trap: Choosing photoperiodism because both involve light. Day length was not varied here; the light was constant at different intensities.

ox: Wrong. At 200 the rate is only 3.2, and it rises to 5.8 at 400, so the rate is still climbing steeply. A leaf still gaining that much from more light is not saturated.
Wrong. At 400 the rate is 5.8, but it still rises to 7.1 at 600 (a gain of 1.3). The rate is still clearly responding to light here.

Correct. The passage says the rate rises 'up to 600 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, after which the rate plateaued.' The table shows 7.1 at 600 and only 7.3 at 800, a gain of just 0.2. So 600 is the lowest intensity on the plateau.
Wrong. 800 is on the plateau (7.3), but it is not the lowest intensity there. The rate at 600 (7.1) is already almost the same, so saturation began at 600.

p: Photosynthesis uses light to make sugar and release oxygen. More light usually means a faster rate. But the leaf has only a limited number of enzymes and electron carriers to process that light.

Once those are working at full speed, extra light adds almost nothing. The graph flattens. That flat region is called the plateau, or light saturation. The 'lowest' intensity on the plateau is where the curve first flattens.

bp1015_0.plain: Think of a checkout line with a fixed number of cashiers. Once every cashier is busy, more customers arriving does not speed up the line.
mem: Plateau means adding more of the input no longer raises the output.
Find saturation where the gains shrink to almost nothing between neighboring points.
The word 'lowest' means pick the first point on the flat part, not the highest value.
bp1015_0.sc: Compare the gaps between neighbors: 3.2 to 5.8 (+2.6), 5.8 to 7.1 (+1.3), 7.1 to 7.3 (+0.2). The gain collapses after 600.
bp1015_0.trap: Picking 800 because it has the highest number. The question asks where the plateau starts, not where the maximum value is.

fm.f: Gain = rate at higher intensity - rate at lower intensity, where rate = O₂ evolution in µmol/g/min
fm.why: A tiny gain means the curve has flattened.
fm.nc: Subtract tenths: 73 - 71 = 2, so 0.2.

ox: Wrong. The passage only says 'fully expanded spinach leaves' were used. It never says older leaves were excluded, so this is invented detail.

Correct. The passage says 'All other variables—temperature (25 °C), CO₂ concentration (400 ppm), and leaf temperature—were held constant.' Holding CO₂ fixed at 400 ppm means a change in O₂ evolution cannot be blamed on CO₂.
Wrong. Light intensity was the independent variable. The passage says leaves were exposed to four intensities (200, 400, 600 and 800), so it was changed on purpose, not held constant.
Wrong. A Clark-type electrode was the measuring tool for oxygen. The passage never says it was varied between replicates, and varying it would add error, not remove it.

p: In a fair experiment you change one thing on purpose. That is the independent variable. Here it is light intensity. The thing you measure is the dependent variable. Here it is O₂ evolution.
Everything else must stay the same. Those are controlled variables. If they stay constant, any change in the result can be blamed on the one thing you changed.

bp1015_1.plain: To test whether a new fertilizer works, you give every plant the same water and sun. Only the fertilizer differs.
mem: Independent variable: what the researcher changes (light).
Dependent variable: what is measured (O₂ evolution).
Controlled variables: what is kept the same (temperature 25 °C, CO₂ 400 ppm).
Look for the phrase 'held constant' in the passage.
bp1015_1.trap: Choosing the 600 option because 600 is the plateau value. That confuses the independent variable (varied) with a controlled one.

ox: Wrong. 50.0 % would mean 3.2 rose to 4.8. The table gives 5.8, which is a bigger rise.
Correct. Percent increase = change divided by starting value. Change = 5.8 - 3.2 = 2.6. Then 2.6 / 3.2 = 0.8125, which is about 81.3 %.
Wrong. 120 % would mean the rate more than doubled (3.2 to 7.04). The table shows 5.8 at 400, not about 7.
Wrong. 150 % would mean 3.2 rose to 8.0. That is higher than any value in the table, so it cannot be right.

p: Percent increase tells you how big a change is compared with where you started. You take the new value minus the old value. Then you divide by the OLD value. Then you multiply by 100.
The starting value is always the denominator. Here the starting value is the rate at 200, which is 3.2.

bp1015_2.plain: If your allowance goes from $3 to $6, it went up by $3, which is 100 percent of the $3 you started with.
mem: Percent change = (new - old) / old x 100.
Always divide by the starting value.
Sanity check: 100 % increase means doubling.

fm.f: Percent increase = (new - old) / old x 100, where old = rate at 200 and new = rate at 400
fm.why: We are comparing a change to the starting rate.

bp1015_2.sc: Doubling 3.2 gives 6.4. 5.8 is a bit less than double, so the answer must be a bit under 100 %. Only 81.3 % fits.
bp1015_2.trap: Dividing by the wrong number or forgetting to divide at all. The denominator must be the 200 value, 3.2.

ox: Wrong. This IS supported. The table rises from 3.2 to 5.8 to 7.1 as light goes from 200 to 600, and the passage says rate increases 'up to 600.'
Wrong. This IS supported. Going from 600 to 800 raises the rate only from 7.1 to 7.3, which is not a significant increase, and the passage says the rate 'plateaued.'

Correct. This is NOT supported. Equal steps in light give unequal steps in rate: +2.6 from 200 to 400, +1.3 from 400 to 600, +0.2 from 600 to 800. A straight line would give equal steps, so the relationship is not linear.
Wrong. This IS supported. The passage itself says the plateau 'indicat[es] a light-saturated response,' and the table shows 7.1 then 7.3.

p: A linear relationship means equal steps in the input give equal steps in the output. A saturating curve rises fast at first and then levels off.
In this data each step of 200 in light gives a smaller gain than the last. That shrinking gain is the signature of saturation.

bp1015_3.plain: Filling a glass with a hose: the water level climbs, then stops rising when the glass is full.
mem: Check equal steps in the table to test linearity.
A plateau means the relationship is not linear.
For NOT supported questions, three options are true and one is false.
bp1015_3.trap: Skipping the 'NOT' in the question and picking a true statement. Mark each option true or false first.

ox: Correct. Between 600 and 800 the rate goes only from 7.1 to 7.3 even though light is higher. So light is no longer the limit. Later steps such as electron transport and carbon fixation, which have a fixed capacity, set the speed.
Wrong. Photon supply did not stop. The intensity rose from 600 to 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, so more light arrived. The question is why the rate did not respond.
Wrong. If Photosystem II were destroyed the rate would fall sharply. The table shows 7.3 at 800, slightly higher than 7.1, so there is no collapse.
Wrong. The electrode recorded 7.3 at 800, which is above 7.1. That shows it can read values higher than 7.1, so a detection limit does not explain the plateau.

p: Photosynthesis is a chain of steps. Light is absorbed first. Then electrons move along carriers, and later the cell uses CO₂ to build sugar.
The slowest step controls the whole chain. At low light, light absorption is the slowest step. At high light, the later steps become the slowest, so more light does nothing.

bp1015_4.plain: An assembly line moves only as fast as its slowest helper. Delivering more parts to the first helper does not help.
mem: Rate is limited by the slowest step.
Low light: light limits. High light: electron transport or carbon fixation limits.
A plateau is different from a decline. Damage would lower the rate.
bp1015_4.trap: Blaming photon supply or photodamage. More light was supplied, and the rate did not fall.

ox: Wrong. 1700 is the supplement group at week 4, not week 8. Read the row labeled Week 8.
Correct. Table 1, row 'Week 8', column 'Supplement Mean RMR' reads '1755 ± 110.' The mean is the number before the ± sign, so 1755 kcal/day.
Wrong. 1650 is the supplement group at baseline, before the 8 weeks of treatment.
Wrong. 1670 is the placebo group mean at week 8. The question asks about the supplement group.

p: To read a table, match the right row to the right column. Rows here are time points. Columns are groups.
In 'mean ± SD', the first number is the mean (the average). The number after ± is the standard deviation, which describes how spread out the individual values are.

bp1017_0.plain: It is like finding a seat in a theater: you need the right row and the right seat number.
mem: Mean is the number before ±.
Match both the row (time) and the column (group).
SD shows spread, not the average.
bp1017_0.trap: Grabbing the right column but the wrong row (week 4) or the right row but the wrong column (placebo).

ox: Correct. The passage says participants 'were randomly assigned to either the supplement group (n=12) or a placebo group (n=12).' Random assignment to a treatment and a placebo is the hallmark of a randomized controlled trial.
Wrong. A cohort study only observes groups that differ naturally in exposure. Here the researchers gave the supplement and assigned people at random.
Wrong. A case-control study starts with people who already have an outcome and looks back at their history. Nobody here was selected by outcome.
Wrong. A cross-sectional study measures everyone once at a single time. This study measured RMR at baseline, week 4 and week 8.

p: In a randomized controlled trial (RCT), researchers assign people to groups by chance and give one group a treatment and the other a placebo (a fake treatment). Random assignment makes the groups similar so the treatment is the main difference.
Observational studies only watch. They do not assign treatments.

bp1017_1.plain: Flipping a coin to decide who gets the real pill and who gets the sugar pill is an RCT.
mem: Random assignment plus intervention equals RCT.
Cohort: follow groups forward, observing only.
Case-control: start with the outcome and look back.
Cross-sectional: one snapshot in time.
bp1017_1.trap: Thinking a longitudinal (repeated over time) study must be a cohort study. Repeated measures can also be part of an RCT.

ox: Wrong. 4.5 % of 1650 is about 74, but the actual rise is 105. So 4.5 % is too small.
Correct. Rise = 1755 - 1650 = 105 kcal/day. Percent = 105 / 1650 x 100, which is about 6.4 %.
Wrong. 8.0 % of 1650 is 132. The actual rise of 105 is smaller than that.
Wrong. 10.2 % of 1650 is about 168. The actual rise of 105 is far smaller.

p: Percent change compares a change to the starting value. Baseline is the starting value measured before treatment.
Subtract baseline from the later value. Divide by baseline. Multiply by 100.

bp1017_2.plain: If a 100-dollar item rises to 106 dollars, that is a 6 percent increase.
mem: Baseline is the denominator.
Estimate by checking 10 % of the baseline first.
Percent change = change / baseline x 100.

fm.f: Percent increase = (week 8 mean - baseline mean) / baseline mean x 100, where means are the supplement group RMR in kcal/day
fm.why: The change is compared with the starting value.
fm.nc: 10 % of 1650 is 165. 105 is a bit over 60 % of 165, so the answer is about 6.4 %.

bp1017_2.sc: 10 % of 1650 is 165. The rise of 105 is well under that, which rules out 8.0 % and 10.2 %.
bp1017_2.trap: Using the week 8 value as the denominator or picking a rounded-looking larger number.

ox: Wrong. This IS supported. The supplement group rose from 1650 to 1700 to 1755.
Wrong. This IS supported. The placebo group rose slightly from 1640 to 1655 to 1670.
Wrong. This IS supported. The supplement group rose 105 (1755 - 1650) and the placebo group rose 30 (1670 - 1640), so the supplement rise was larger.
Correct. This is NOT supported. The supplement means went up at every time point (1650, 1700, 1755). A decrease would show values falling.

p: NOT questions need each option checked against the data. Three options will be true. One will be false.
Direction matters. Increase means the later value is bigger than the earlier one.

bp1017_3.plain: If your savings go from 10 to 20 to 30 dollars, saying they fell is simply wrong.
mem: Test each option against the table one by one.
Compare changes from each group's own baseline.
The placebo group can also change a little.
bp1017_3.trap: Picking the placebo statement because a placebo is supposed to do nothing. The table shows it still rose by 30.

ox: Correct. Supplement change = 1755 - 1650 = +105. Placebo change = 1670 - 1640 = +30. The difference in change is 105 - 30 = 75 kcal/day.
Wrong. 85 is 1755 - 1670, the gap between the week 8 means. That ignores that the groups began at different baselines (1650 versus 1640).
Wrong. 105 is only the supplement group's own change. The placebo's 30 was not subtracted.
Wrong. 30 is only the placebo group's change. The question wants the difference between the two changes.

p: To judge a treatment, compare how much each group changed from its own starting point. The placebo group shows what happens without the treatment.
So first find each group's change, then subtract the placebo change from the treatment change.

bp1017_4.plain: If you gain 5 points on a test and your friend gains 2, you gained 3 more points than your friend.
mem: Change = later value - own baseline.
Treatment effect = treatment change - placebo change.
Do not just compare final values.

fm.f: Difference = (supplement week 8 - supplement baseline) - (placebo week 8 - placebo baseline)
fm.why: Each group is compared with its own starting point.

bp1017_4.trap: Subtracting the week 8 means directly (85) and skipping baseline corrections.

ox: Wrong. At 200 the table shows only 15 µmol O₂ (g leaf)⁻¹ h⁻¹, the lowest of the four values.
Wrong. At 400 the mean is 28, which is less than 35 at 600 and 45 at 800.
Wrong. At 600 the mean is 35, still below 45 at 800.
Correct. The table lists 45 µmol O₂ (g leaf)⁻¹ h⁻¹ at 800, the largest of 15, 28, 35 and 45. The passage also says 'Oxygen production rose at every successive light intensity tested.'

concept.t: Reading the maximum in a data table
p: A table lists one measured value per condition. To find the highest, scan the value column and pick the biggest number, then read across to its condition.
Here the condition is light intensity (how much light hits the leaf) and the value is oxygen made by the leaf each hour. Only the four tested intensities can be answered from the data.

bp1029_0.plain: It is like checking four test scores and naming the day with the top score. You only look at the numbers you were given.
mem: Highest value in the column gives the answer; do not guess what happens beyond the tested range.
Photosynthesis rate is often measured as O₂ released.
More light usually raises the rate until another factor limits it, but only the data tell you where.
bp1029_0.trap: Assuming the curve must level off before 800. The passage says oxygen rose at every step, so the top tested intensity is the highest.

ox: Wrong. Light intensity is what the researchers deliberately changed (200, 400, 600, 800), so it is the independent variable.
Correct. Oxygen production (µmol O₂ (g leaf)⁻¹ h⁻¹) is the thing measured in response to the changed light, so it is the dependent variable.
Wrong. The measurement period was fixed at 10 minutes for the study, so it was not changing with treatment.
Wrong. Only spinach was used, so species does not vary. A constant cannot be a dependent variable.

p: The independent variable is the one the experimenter changes on purpose. The dependent variable is the outcome that is measured to see whether it responds.
Everything else is held constant (a control or constant). In this study the passage says temperature and CO₂ stayed the same and only light changed.

bp1029_1.plain: If you change how much water a plant gets and watch its height, water is what you change and height is what you measure.
mem: Independent = what you change; dependent = what you measure.
Dependent variable goes on the y-axis, independent on the x-axis.
Held-constant factors (temperature, CO₂) are controls.
bp1029_1.trap: Picking light intensity because it is the main topic. The question asks what is measured as the outcome, not what is manipulated.

ox: Correct. Rise = 45 - 15 = 30. Percent increase = 30/15 x 100 = 200%.
Wrong. 250% would need a final value of 15 + 37.5 = 52.5, but the table says 45 at 800.
Wrong. 300% would give 15 + 45 = 60. The table value is 45, so the increase is 30, not 45. This confuses 'three times' (45 is 3x15) with a 300% increase.
Wrong. 350% would give 67.5, far above the 45 in the table.

p: Percent increase tells how much something grew compared with where it started. You subtract the start from the end, divide by the start, then multiply by 100.
Fold change is the end divided by the start. A 3-fold value (3x) equals a 200% increase, because the original 100% is not counted as increase.

bp1029_2.plain: If your allowance goes from $15 to $45, you now have three times as much, but you got $30 extra, which is double your old amount.

fm.f: Percent increase = (final - initial) / initial x 100, where final = oxygen at 800, initial = oxygen at 200
fm.why: It compares the change with the starting value.
fm.nc: 30 is exactly 2 times 15, so the answer is 200%.

bp1029_2.sc: Fold change minus 1, times 100. Here 45/15 = 3, so 3 - 1 = 2, which is 200%.
bp1029_2.trap: Answering 300% because the final value is 3 times the start. Percent increase subtracts the original 100% first.
mem: Percent increase = (final - initial) / initial x 100.
3 times as large = 200% increase, not 300%.
Check: fold change minus 1, times 100.

ox: Wrong. This is supported, so it is not the answer. The table gives 45 at 800 and 15 at 200, and 45 = 3 x 15.
Wrong. This is supported. The table gives 35 at 600 and 28 at 400, and 35 is greater than 28.
Correct. This is the unsupported statement. The table shows 35 at 600 and 45 at 800, so oxygen was still rising, and the passage says rates rose at every step and nothing above 800 was tested.
Wrong. This is supported. The values 15, 28, 35, 45 go up at every step, matching the passage.

p: In a 'NOT supported' question, three choices are true according to the data and one is false or unprovable. Check each choice against the table and cross off the true ones.
The leftover choice is the answer. Claims about a plateau need data showing no further rise.

bp1029_3.plain: It is like comparing four statements and keeping only the one that the evidence does not back up.
mem: For NOT questions, test each option and eliminate the true ones.
A plateau needs the last values to be about equal; here 35 to 45 is still a rise.
Do not extrapolate beyond the tested range.
bp1029_3.trap: Flipping the question and choosing a statement that is supported. Keep 'NOT' in mind while checking each option.

ox: Correct. In the light reactions, photosystem II splits water (oxidizes it), giving O₂, protons and electrons. That O₂ is what leaves the leaf and is measured as 'oxygen evolution'.
Wrong. Rubisco fixes CO₂ into sugar in the Calvin cycle. This step consumes CO₂ and does not release O₂.
Wrong. Reduction of NADP⁺ to NADPH stores electrons. It uses electrons, it does not make O₂.
Wrong. Glycolysis breaks glucose down in the cytoplasm and does not release O₂ or need light.

p: Photosynthesis has two stages. In the light reactions, light energy is used to pull electrons off water. This happens at photosystem II, a protein complex in the thylakoid membrane, and it releases O₂ as a by-product.
In the Calvin cycle, CO₂ is built into sugar using the ATP and NADPH made earlier.

bp1029_4.plain: Plants break water apart to get electrons, and the leftover oxygen floats away as waste.
mem: O₂ from photosynthesis comes from water, not from CO₂.
Photosystem II splits water; photosystem I makes NADPH.
Calvin cycle uses CO₂, ATP and NADPH to make sugar.
bp1029_4.trap: Picking the Calvin cycle because CO₂ is involved. The O₂ atoms come from water in the light reactions.

ox: Wrong. Red has a chlorophyll absorbance of 0.45, the lowest of the three rows, so it is not the highest.

Correct. The table lists chlorophyll (absorbance) as Red 0.45, Blue 0.60, White 0.50. The passage also says 'blue light significantly increased chlorophyll content compared to red and white.' Blue's 0.60 is the largest value.
Wrong. White has 0.50, which is higher than red (0.45) but lower than blue (0.60).
Wrong. The values are not tied. Blue's 0.60 is clearly the largest, so one treatment does stand out.

p: A table has rows (each treatment) and columns (each thing measured). To answer 'which is highest', find the right column first, then compare the numbers in only that column.
Here the column is Chlorophyll (absorbance). Absorbance is how much light a sample soaks up. More chlorophyll soaks up more light, so a bigger number means more chlorophyll.

bp1032_0.plain: It is like checking a scoreboard: you look only at the column for the event you care about, then pick the biggest number.
mem: Pick the correct column before comparing rows.
Higher absorbance means more pigment in the sample.
Different outcomes can have different winners.
bp1032_0.trap: Mixing up columns. Red wins growth rate (0.12) and biomass (120 mg), but not chlorophyll.

ox: Correct. The passage says 'The study employed a randomized block design with five replicates per treatment group.' A block design groups similar units together so that differences between blocks are removed from the error, which controls variability.
Wrong. A completely randomized design assigns units to treatments with no grouping, so it does not remove variability between groups of plants. The passage names a block design, not this one.
Wrong. A factorial design tests two or more factors together (for example light color and temperature). This study changed only one factor, light wavelength.
Wrong. A split-plot design is for factors applied at different levels, such as whole plots and sub-plots. The passage never describes this, and states 'randomized block'.

p: Variability means that plants differ from each other for reasons that have nothing to do with the treatment. A block is a group of similar units, such as plants on the same shelf. Each block gets every treatment, in random order.
Because the comparison happens inside each block, the shelf-to-shelf differences are separated out. That makes the treatment effect easier to see.

bp1032_1.plain: It is like comparing three fertilizers by testing all three in every garden bed, so a sunny bed does not make one fertilizer look better.
mem: Block = group similar units, randomize within each block.
Factorial = more than one factor tested together.
The passage text names the design; look for it.
bp1032_1.trap: Picking factorial because it sounds more advanced. Only one factor (light wavelength) was varied.

ox: Wrong. 25% comes from dividing the difference (0.15) by the blue value (0.60). The starting value is red, not blue.
Correct. Percent increase = (0.60 - 0.45) / 0.45 = 0.15 / 0.45 = 1/3, which is about 33%. Red (0.45) is the baseline and blue (0.60) is the new value, both from the table.
Wrong. 40% does not match 0.15 / 0.45. It would need blue to be 0.63.
Wrong. 50% would need blue to be 0.675, since 0.45 x 1.5 = 0.675. The table says 0.60.

p: Percent increase tells you how much bigger a new number is compared to a starting number. You always divide the change by the starting number, called the baseline.
Here the question says blue relative to red, so red (0.45) is the baseline.

bp1032_2.plain: If a pizza goes from 3 slices to 4, you gained 1 slice, and 1 out of your original 3 is one third.
mem: Percent change = change / baseline x 100.
Baseline is the 'relative to' value.
Fractions like 1/3 = 33% and 1/4 = 25% are worth memorizing.

fm.f: Percent increase = (new - baseline) / baseline x 100, where new = blue chlorophyll absorbance and baseline = red chlorophyll absorbance
fm.why: The question asks for a change relative to red, so red is the baseline.
fm.nc: Multiply both by 100: 15 / 45 simplifies to 1/3.

bp1032_2.sc: Compute 15/45 by removing the decimals, then simplify to 1/3.
bp1032_2.trap: Dividing by the blue value (0.15/0.60 = 25%) instead of the red baseline.

ox: Wrong. This statement is supported: the table gives blue 0.60, the highest chlorophyll absorbance.
Wrong. This statement is supported: red has 120 mg, the highest biomass in the table.
Wrong. This statement is supported: growth rates run from 0.10 to 0.12, a spread of 0.02 cm/day.

Correct. This is the unsupported statement. Red has the highest growth rate (0.12) and biomass (120), but its chlorophyll absorbance (0.45) is the lowest of the three. It does not lead on all three outcomes.

p: A NOT question asks you to find the one false statement. Three options are true and one is false. Check each option against the table and mark it true or false.
The false one is the answer, even though it may sound the most plausible.

bp1032_3.plain: It is like a quiz where three facts are true and you have to spot the fib.
mem: In NOT questions, the answer is the false statement.
Check every column before accepting 'all' or 'always' claims.
Words like 'all three' are easy to disprove with one counterexample.
bp1032_3.trap: Seeing red lead two columns and assuming it leads all three. One lower value breaks an 'all' claim.

ox: Wrong. Photon energy E = hc / wavelength, so a longer wavelength gives less energy. Red at 660 nm is lower in energy than blue at 450 nm.

Correct. E = hc / wavelength, so energy is inversely related to wavelength. Blue (450 nm) is shorter than red (660 nm), so each blue photon carries more energy. The ratio is 660/450 = 22/15, about 1.47 times.
Wrong. Visible light covers a range of wavelengths (and energies). Blue and red are both visible, but their energies differ.
Wrong. Intensity sets how many photons arrive, not how much energy each one has. Energy per photon depends on wavelength (or frequency).

p: Light comes in packets called photons. Each photon has energy E = hc / wavelength, where h is Planck's constant, c is the speed of light, and wavelength is the distance between wave peaks.
Because wavelength is in the denominator, a shorter wavelength means more energy. Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red, so blue photons are more energetic.

bp1032_4.plain: Short, tight waves are like fast, hard-hitting punches. Long, lazy waves are like gentle taps.
mem: Shorter wavelength = higher frequency = higher energy.
Visible order by energy: violet and blue highest, red lowest.
Intensity = number of photons, not energy each.

fm.f: E = hc / wavelength, where E = energy per photon, h = Planck's constant, c = speed of light
fm.v: wavelength red = 660 nm, wavelength blue = 450 nm
fm.why: The constants h and c cancel in a ratio, so only the wavelengths matter.

bp1032_4.trap: Thinking longer wavelength means more energy, or that brighter light means higher-energy photons.

ox: Wrong. At 400 nm the O2 production is 18.7, lower than the 23.9 at 450 nm.
Correct. Table 1 shows the highest O2 production, 23.9 µmol O2 mg Chl-1 h-1, at 450 nm. The passage also says the response had "peak oxygen production at 450 nm."
Wrong. At 500 nm the value is 19.5, which is close but still below 23.9.
Wrong. At 600 nm the value is only 13.1, much lower than 23.9.

concept.t: Finding a maximum in a table
p: Rate of oxygen evolution is how much O2 the algae release over time. A higher number means faster photosynthesis, because photosynthesis releases O2 when water is split.
To find the best condition, scan the output column and choose the largest value, then read the matching row.

bp1038_0.plain: It is like reading a scoreboard: the winner is the row with the highest score.
mem: More O2 released means a faster light reaction.
Read the biggest number, then match its row.
Chlorophylls absorb blue and red strongly, and green least.
bp1038_0.sc: Circle the highest number in the output column first, then read across.
bp1038_0.trap: Picking a close value (19.5 at 500 nm) because it looks plausible instead of comparing all five values.

ox: Correct. To isolate wavelength, change only wavelength and hold everything else fixed. The passage did exactly this by using "a constant photon flux density of 200 µmol m-2 s-1" at all five wavelengths, so any difference in O2 can be linked to wavelength.
Wrong. Changing both together confounds the two variables. A change in O2 could be due to either one, so you could not attribute it to wavelength.
Wrong. This isolates the effect of intensity, not wavelength. It answers a different question.
Wrong. A dark control shows O2 use from respiration with no light. It does not compare wavelengths, so it cannot isolate their effect.
